claims.text: The starting material is a nominally equiatomic WTaVTi refractory high-entropy alloy.
The as-cast WTaVTi precursor has directionally solidified W/Ta-rich dendrites and Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels.
Immersion of the precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h will produce a bicontinuous, directionally aligned composite.
Liquid-metal dealloying selectively extracts Ti from the interdendritic regions and forms nearly pure FCC Cu channels.
W, Ta, and V left by dealloying form BCC refractory-high-entropy-alloy ligaments.
The resulting composite contains approximately 63.6 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments and 36.4 vol.% FCC Cu channels.
A spontaneously formed, approximately 300 nm thick W-rich interlayer lies at the RHEA/Cu interfaces.
Ti has a negative heat of mixing with Cu.
The favorable Ti–Cu mixing interaction causes Ti to preferentially exchange with Cu and dissolve during dealloying.
W, Ta, and V are sufficiently immiscible with Cu to remain as stable RHEA ligaments.
W and Cu have a strongly positive heat of mixing.
The positive W–Cu heat of mixing causes formation of a W-rich interlayer that passivates the interface and arrests further exchange.
The W-rich interlayer ensures strong bonding between the RHEA and Cu phases.
The aligned Cu channels act as efficient thermal conduits.
The complex RHEA lattice resists helium-induced swelling.
The dealloyed composite will have substantially higher thermal conductivity, particularly above approximately 650 °C, than the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor and pure W.
The dealloyed composite will exhibit lower helium-induced swelling than pure W or conventional W–Cu composites under 25 keV He+ irradiation.
The dealloyed composite will show delayed blister formation under low-energy He+ irradiation.
The continuous RHEA network will preserve high mechanical durability.
Prior evidence supports improved thermal conductivity and irradiation resistance in this system.
